wa_north_face_3.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
wa_north_face_3.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just under a mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, leave the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and work up into the next gully south, the one that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.
hazards: loose rock in the Concord-Lexington gully
lingering firm snow or névé in the upper gully into early summer — axe or traction useful
the descent uses slung horns rather than fixed anchors, so carry spare webbing
wa_north_face_3.baseFinding: The route does not start from the high point of the col. From the crest, move slightly west and drop a couple of feet: the first pitch begins at an obvious slanting, right-leaning crack in the Lexington side of the notch, and the 5.7 crux is the very first thing you climb — awkward moves straight off the ground. Follow the leaning crack for about 15 to 20 feet and it eases into stemming up a chimney at around 5.6. If your first moves are easy you are probably on the Concord wall opposite, which is the South Face of Concord and starts by walking gravelly ledges rather than pulling on a crack. A hard start on a right-leaning crack, just below and west of the col, is the confirmation.

wa_north_face_3.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
wa_north_face_3.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.
hazards: firm snow in the gully below the col
moat where snow meets the Lexington wall
SR-20 closed in winter — no vehicle access until reopening
wa_north_face_3.baseFinding: With snow in the col the slanting crack that starts the route can be partly buried, and the couple of feet of drop west from the high point may instead be a step down into a moat. The feature to hold onto is that the start is on the Lexington side, slightly west of and just below the crest, at a right-leaning crack, and the hardest climbing of the first pitch is immediately off the deck. If snow has filled the crack's base, expect to start higher up it than the summer start and to be dealing with wet rock for the first body length.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: Boat crossing of Ross Lake needed; a long multi-day approach with a retreat measured in days
Abandoned, brushy Freezeout Creek trail; tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft
Steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the walk
Awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face
Several unmarked lines on one wall; descent by the east ridge and snow finger, not the route reversed
wa_north_face_left_buttress.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face
Several unmarked lines on one wall; descent by the east ridge and snow finger, not the route reversed
Very remote, multi-day approach with no quick rescue
wa_north_face_left_buttress.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Wildfires close this road and parts of the northern wilderness in some summers, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
bivy.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
bivy.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
bivy.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
bivy.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
bivy.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
hazards: Very long high walk of about 27 miles, a 3-5 day trip with no shortcut
Harts Pass road is single lane, steep and exposed; usually opens only in July; wildfire can close it
Snow lingering on north-facing traverses into August; sparse water along the crest
Wind and cold on the open crest, far from the car if weather turns
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face; descent by the east ridge and snow finger

wa_north_ridge_2.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
camps: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_north_ridge_2.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
hazards: Unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
Chilliwack River crossing by hand-operated cable car or a ford
Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack is the riskier option
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge
wa_north_ridge_2.baseFinding:
The base is the broad toe of the ridge, and you find it by walking south off the pass until the path dies. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is stay on the crest rather than follow any marked line.

So the fog test is a handrail test, and it is the best kind: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

Arrival at the start: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

What the upper ridge is like, because it decides whether you come back this way: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

And the other thing this ridge is: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told not to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.

wa_north_ridge_2.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_north_ridge_2.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail
Whatcom Glacier loop back to the pass needs glacier travel gear
wa_north_ridge_2.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive at Whatcom Pass, the base test is identical: leave the maintained trail, head directly south on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

The one thing this side changes, and it is a logistics fact rather than a navigation one: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

How you know you are at the pass and not at a camp below it: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.

wa_north_ridge_3.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear right into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
camps: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
wa_north_ridge_3.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. It sees far less traffic than the South Buttress, the peak's classic line.
hazards: Loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch with marginal protection to gain the North Ridge Notch from the basin
Loose rock and poor gear on the notch-gaining pitch; the first two pitches of the ridge carry the worst rock, with a shifting flake
Creek crossing and brushy climbers' path low on the approach
Route-finding in the boulder field: bear right into the basin under the notch, not left toward the other route's gully
Descent drops into the notch and down a different route's four-rappel line; a more direct West Ridge descent is rockier
wa_north_ridge_3.baseFinding:
At the boulder field, bear right and north into the basin beneath the north ridge notch, rather than left toward the south buttress gully. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

The route's real base is the notch, and getting to it is itself a pitch: from the basin, A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch gains the north ridge notch. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, and this pitch should be treated as the technical and psychological crux of the approach, not of the ridge above it.

So the test is blunt: if the hardest, scariest thing you have done is the pitch that got you to the notch, you are on the right route. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

Arrival: a notch, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

The northern alternative, which arrives at the same notch from the other side: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb two or three short pitches of low fifth class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

Descent does not reverse the approach pitch all the way: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors and continuing down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Rainy Pass and Porcupine Creek into the basin northwest of the peak

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_north_ridge_3.notes: From Rainy Pass, follow the PCT north for about twenty minutes and leave it before the Porcupine Creek bridge, climbing through timber into the basin northwest of the peak. Two or three short low-fifth pitches reach the North Ridge notch. Longer than the south-side basin, but on cleaner rock to the notch; parties camped near Rainy Pass or combining objectives use it.
hazards: Two or three short low-fifth-class pitches to gain the notch from the north, on terrain that has no stored protection details
Off-trail climb through timber into the basin northwest of the peak, leaving the PCT before the Porcupine Creek bridge
Loose rock on the lower pitches of the ridge, with the worst quality in the first two pitches above the notch
Descent still goes to the notch and down the south-side rappel line, a long way around to the Rainy Pass trailhead
Considerably longer approach than the south basin

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Rainy Pass, the PCT north and the ridge above Porcupine Creek
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: Follow the PCT north from Rainy Pass about a mile and a half, to just before the Porcupine Creek bridge, then climb the ridge northeast for about two miles to the base. The shorter way, with the cleaner gully to the base.
hazards: Approach gullies hold most of the loose material; rockfall from loose blocks and flakes
Loose rock is the biggest climbing problem on all terrain, with quality varying across the steep jointed granite
Off-trail climb up the ridge northeast from the PCT beyond the Porcupine Creek crossing
Descent uses three rappels on the north ridge or an 80 ft rappel southwest; anchors must be tested and loose blocks watched for

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin below Cutthroat Peak. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. On this approach the lake is on the way: the trail continues past it and climbs to Cutthroat Pass, from where the crest leads south about a mile to the base of the North Ridge. From the Rainy Pass side it is off the route entirely.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: The eastern way: on trail most of the way, to Cutthroat Lake and up to Cutthroat Pass, then south along the crest for about a mile.
hazards: Rotten rock on the final ridge-crest approach from Cutthroat Pass
Loose rock is the biggest climbing problem on all terrain, with quality varying across the steep jointed granite
Rockfall from loose blocks and flakes in the gullies on the descent back toward the pass
Long approach with about 2,300 ft of gain via Cutthroat Lake and the pass
Descent uses three rappels on the north ridge or an 80 ft rappel southwest; test every anchor

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Lyman Lakes basin to the south flank
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: Access is the hard part and it has changed. The classic way in is by passenger ferry up Lake Chelan and a village shuttle to the Railroad Creek trail, then a long valley walk to the Lyman Lakes basin — but that corridor has been shut by flood and landslide damage with no near-term reopening, so plan instead on the longer route in from the Phelps Creek side over Spider Gap, which is eleven or twelve miles one way and involves glacier travel with an axe. Either way this is a camp-in-the-basin objective, not a day out. Maintained tread effectively ends at the lakes; everything above is picked by eye with no path and no cairns. It is commonly paired with the lower summit less than a mile to its south from the same camp.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.season: Late July to September; axe early
hazards: Unconsolidated talus and scree with no path, releasing rock onto anyone below
Snowfield at the foot of the south flank persists through late summer and may need an axe early in the season
The lower southwest ridge is cliffed and drops off; it is not an ascent line
Wet, lichen-covered rock near the summit
Extremely remote; the corridor to Railroad Creek has been closed since the 2025 storm damage, so access is uncertain
Afternoon thunderstorms and long emergency response times
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.baseFinding: From the Lyman Lakes basin the mountain shows as a broad talus flank above open meadow, and the base is a specific, findable thing rather than a general slope: a snowfield lying at roughly 7,000 ft at the foot of that flank, which survives into late summer most years and is visible as a white patch from the camps when you look up from the lake. Cross the meadow, round onto the south and southeast side, and climb to it. Above the snow a broad ledge leads rightward into the main gully, and the gully takes you to a notch on the crest from which the ridge runs to the top. Do not try to gain the crest lower down on the southwest side — that ridge is cliffed below the notch and the drop-offs are the reason parties are warned off it. The other thing to keep straight is which summit you are under: a lower, closer peak sits under a mile to the south, and if the ground ahead is easing toward a rounded top rather than steepening into a gully, you are on that one.

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

bivy.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
bivy.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
bivy.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: The Phelps Creek trail to Spider Meadow, over Spider Gap and down to Lyman Lakes, then the same basin to the south flank. No boat needed.
hazards: Glacier travel with moats and crevasses crossing Spider Gap and the Lyman Glacier; ice axe and traction needed even in August
Permanent snowfield below the gap must be crossed
Unconsolidated talus and scree on the south flank, releasing rock onto anyone below
Wet, lichen-covered rock near the summit
Long approach of roughly 11-12 miles one way, in an area affected by fire and road closures
Remote terrain with long emergency response times; afternoon thunderstorms

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
camps: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
hazards: Chilliwack cable-car crossing and Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
About 1,000 ft descending traverse across snow and talus to the buttress, to be regained on the return
Bergschrund on the pocket glacier, crossed via a slabby rock step; crevasse fall risk
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully; natural anchors only
False summit and exposed ridge crest: route-finding risk in fog or whiteout
Fast-moving fog and fickle weather; 2-3 days of travel each way
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is a saddle inside the buttress, at about 6,100 ft, and you get there by losing height first. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 ft descending traverse east across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

So the test in cloud is the shape of the ground, not the view: you go down and east for a thousand feet, then up a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

What going too far looks like: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

Confirm on the climb: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed after the Luna Fire; check the park's fire-closure list for current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, about half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder lower down and farther downstream
Risk of falling into holes hidden in the brush and of separating from a partner
No trail and no cairns; disorienting on the way back down
Bergschrund on the pocket glacier, crossed via a slabby rock step; rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower; false summit and exposed ridge crest in fog
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.baseFinding:
In this drainage the navigation rule is about height, not direction, and it is the one thing that makes the day work. The creek must be forded in places, and fords get harder the lower and farther downstream you are. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

Arrival, which is unambiguous even with no visibility: above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

From there the base test is the same one the northern approach uses: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A real risk peculiar to this approach, recorded because it has happened: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.name: North Fork Entiat over Saska Pass and Snow Brushy Creek
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.notes: A long, largely off-trail approach through burned country for a summit that is barely a scramble. From the North Fork Entiat road end the tread runs up-valley past the Fern Lake spur to the Pyramid Mountain junction, which is the usual last camp with water; fill there, because the drainages between it and the pass are seasonal and often dry. Gain Saska Pass by climbing the drainage directly rather than following the sidehill traverse, which is slower and more tiring across scree. From the pass you lose about 1,500 ft into the Snow Brushy burn, where the tread is gone entirely and ash-covered slopes and fallen snags erase any line, then regain nineteen hundred feet or so out of the creek — that descent and reclimb are what make the day long, not the peak. A separate approach exists up the Entiat River trail and the sheep driveway from the south, also through heavy fire blowdown.
hazards: Loose scree on the headwall below Saska Pass, dangerous for anyone beneath you
Burn-zone deadfall and standing snags with no surviving tread in the Snow Brushy burn
Scarce water above the last creek crossings; the drainages near the pass are seasonal
Steep, loose couloir on the final approach to the crest saddle
Loose talus and scree on the class 2-3 summit slopes
Long, remote, mostly off-trail approach with little cell coverage
wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.baseFinding: The base is the saddle on the Chelan Mountains crest immediately south of the peak, reached by a steep couloir of loose rock, and the thing to know before you get there is that the true summit is hidden from it. Standing on the saddle you see a rocky bump close by to the south — a point just over 7,760 ft — and a broad, easy-angled slope running north. The bump is not the mountain and is only a short side trip for the view; the slope is your line. Turn north and climb the south-facing talus, keeping to the west side of the crest where the scrambling stays easiest, and the top only reveals itself in the last few hundred feet. The rock underfoot changes noticeably as you go: poor scree low down where the burn ends, then firmer blocks on the crest that make a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk. If the ground ahead drops away toward the Emerald Peak basin instead of rising, you have crossed the crest too far east.

wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.name: Entiat River trail and Snow Brushy Creek to Borealis Pass

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.notes: From the Entiat River trailhead just past Cottonwood Campground, walk the Entiat River trail about six and a half miles to the Snow Brushy Creek trail, then follow it up-valley about five miles; the creek crossing there is a reliable place for water. A faint, sometimes hard-to-follow trail branches north and climbs to Borealis Pass in about a mile, below the easy south slopes of the peak. Much of the valley is burned, so expect downed timber.
hazards: Burned valley with downed timber and a faint, sometimes hard-to-follow trail to Borealis Pass
Wildfire burn-zone deadfall and obscured tread on the lower approach
Fire closure and landslide near the river trailhead can block the drive; confirm access
Scarce water above the last creek crossings
Loose talus and scree on the class 2-3 summit slopes
Long, remote approach with little cell coverage

wa_primus_peak_south_ridge.name: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
wa_primus_peak_south_ridge.notes:
This is the way to Primus's south side, and it comes from the opposite side of the mountain to the Thunder Creek approach. From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, cross the North Fork Cascade River, climb the steep root-laced boot path through timber, cross the boulder field around 4,000 ft following cairns on the right side of the talus, and reach the meadows of Eldorado Basin. Continue to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and rope up — it is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year.

From the upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col near 7,800 ft. Parties describe crossing the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility, so plan for it.

Summit day from a Klawatti Col camp: downclimb or make a short rappel of about 50 ft through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier, rope up, and traverse below the south side of Austera's east ridge, rounding its end near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier — probing, because this stretch has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility — to the foot of Primus's south side. Then unrope and walk.

The route crosses the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister, Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers in sequence; Austera Towers is passed and bypassed on a short scree ramp along the glacier's eastern edge.
wa_primus_peak_south_ridge.season: Mid-July through August, when the glacier bridges are most consolidated and whiteout risk is lowest
hazards: A heavily crevassed North Klawatti and McAllister glacier system, especially late season
Thin, unreliable snow bridges by August and September — probe before committing weight
Complex glacier route-finding around Klawatti Col in poor visibility
A short technical step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch that has to be reversed at the end of the day
Extreme remoteness: a multi-day approach with no cell coverage
wa_primus_peak_south_ridge.baseFinding: The one findable feature on this route is the notch at the McALLISTER-Klawatti Col, and it is findable because it is the only place all day you need a rope for rock. It is a step of roughly 50 ft: downclimbed, hand-lined, or rappelled off a sling on a horn or block — there is no fixed hardware. If you have crossed a col without a technical step, you are not through it yet. After the notch, the test is what you are standing on rather than what you can see. You drop onto the Klawatti Glacier, traverse below Austera's east ridge and round its end onto the North Klawatti Glacier. The climbing begins where you take the rope off: snow-covered talus, class 2-3, straight to the 8,508 ft summit. There is no notch, no rib and no marked start above the glacier — the honest answer is that this route has no rock landmark at its base, and the col behind you is what tells you where you are. The negative test is the strong one and it settles the whole peak: the other standard line on Primus is reached from Thunder Creek, and it starts at Lucky Pass — a notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier where the route to Tricouni Peak splits off east. If you are at a pass with a second peak's route leaving it, you are on the east slope and you came up the wrong valley for this route. The two lines are on opposite sides of the mountain and share no ground below the summit. And watch the false summit whatever side you came from: a false top stands around 8,270 ft and is passed on climber's-left. A high point reached without traversing round anything is not the summit.

wa_primus_peak_south_ridge.name: Thunder Creek and the Borealis Glacier: the east ridge from Lucky Pass
wa_primus_peak_south_ridge.notes:
The other way onto Primus comes from the north, and it finishes on a different line: the east ridge, not this route's south side. From Colonial Creek Campground on the North Cascades Highway, walk the Thunder Creek Trail about six miles to McAllister Camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek there has washed out, so expect to ford cold, fast water or hunt for a log crossing.

Across the creek, a faint, steep boot path climbs the long, brushy lower north ridge of Tricouni Peak to the toe of the Borealis Glacier near 6,000 ft, where there is good camping. From camp, climb the glacier along its eastern edge, keeping clear of the icefall in its middle, to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni near 7,200 ft, and follow the east ridge to the summit on class 3 ground.

The brush on the ridge above Thunder Creek is slow going in either direction, and worse carrying skis or a long pack.
hazards: An unbridged ford of Thunder Creek at McAllister Camp
A steep, brushy boot path that is easy to lose on the ridge above Thunder Creek
An icefall in the middle of the Borealis Glacier that has to be skirted
Class 3 ground on the east ridge above Lucky Pass

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
hazards: Aasgard Pass: steep loose scree, with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow and a fatal history
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus in the Core
5.11+ crux on the first pitch, sustained hard crack climbing far above gear
Loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side: one bolted station, then gear and slung naturals; carry webbing to back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.baseFinding:
Fifty feet left of the standard South Face route. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

The first pitch is the check, and it is a brutal one. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

What the first pitch looks like from the ground, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing left-slanting crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

Belay confirmation: pitch one ends at a two-bolt anchor after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

And the named pitch higher up: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

Descent note that affects the approach decision: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet. It is also the fallback when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed. From Lake Viviane, go up and right toward Temple Lake and then up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
hazards: Long approach of about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain via the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Unmarked cross-country travel past the upper lakes to the base of the south face
5.11+ crux on the first pitch, sustained hard crack climbing far above gear
Loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side: one bolted station, then gear and slung naturals; carry webbing to back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit

wa_prusik_peak_sail_away.name: Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass
wa_prusik_peak_sail_away.notes: The usual way in. From the Stuart Lake trailhead walk the Colchuck Lake trail to Colchuck Lake, then climb the loose boulders and scree of Aasgard Pass into the Core Enchantments. Walk down through the basin past Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass and scramble up to the base of the south face; Aasgard is steep and can hold snow into early summer.
hazards: Aasgard Pass is steep loose boulders and scree and can hold snow into early summer
Hidden creek and moat under lingering snow on the pass
Sustained 5.11 climbing with increasingly steep flakes and an overhanging headwall crack finish
Rappels use the shared Solid Gold anchors, two rappels, then a walk-off down the north side and scramble back to the south face base
